questions.q: What distinguishes paper trading from a backtest?
options: Paper trading uses more historical data than a backtest

Paper trading runs the strategy through the real live pipeline (real-time data feed, actual order-generation code, simulated order placement) without committing real capital, rather than replaying data already fully in hand
There is no real difference; they are two names for the same process
Paper trading always produces better results than a backtest
questions.explain: A backtest replays historical data the researcher already fully possesses. Paper trading exercises the actual live infrastructure — data feed, signal code, order generation — in real time, with simulated rather than real order execution.

questions.q: What kind of problem can paper trading catch that even a realistic backtest cannot?
options: Transaction costs, since backtests can never model costs
Infrastructure and data-pipeline issues, such as whether the live feed arrives in the expected format or the strategy behaves sanely around a stale quote or halted symbol
Statistical significance of the Sharpe ratio
Maximum drawdown, since backtests cannot compute drawdown
questions.explain: Paper trading exercises real infrastructure a backtest never touches: the live data feed's actual behavior, the order-generation code running unattended and reliably, and how the strategy handles real-world data glitches that clean historical data doesn't have.

questions.q: In the lesson's worked example, the correlation between backtest-predicted and paper-traded daily returns was 0.957, with a cumulative gap of about -1 percentage point over three months. How should that gap be interpreted?
options: The paper trading system is broken since results don't exactly match the backtest

It quantifies real-world friction (execution delay, slightly worse fills, data quirks) that the backtest could not fully anticipate, while the high correlation shows the strategy is still tracking its intended behavior
A gap of this size means the strategy should be abandoned immediately
The gap has no meaningful interpretation on its own
questions.explain: High correlation confirms the paper-traded strategy is behaving as the backtest expected day to day, while the cumulative gap gives a concrete, quantified estimate of friction the backtest missed — exactly the kind of comparison paper trading is meant to produce.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say there's a real tension in choosing how long to paper trade?
options: There is no tension; longer is always strictly better with no downside
Too short a window gives false confidence due to noise dominating the comparison, while too long a window risks missing the opportunity the strategy was built to capture
Paper trading duration has no effect on the statistical reliability of the comparison
Regulators mandate an exact paper-trading duration for every strategy
questions.explain: A short paper-trading window suffers the same sampling-noise problem discussed in Lesson 25 — the comparison isn't statistically meaningful yet. But paper trading indefinitely risks missing the market opportunity. There's no universal right answer, only honesty about the statistical weight the window can bear.

questions.q: What risk does paper trading fail to rehearse, even when its results closely match the backtest?
options: Market-impact risk — since paper orders never actually move the market, a strategy can behave very differently once real orders of real size interact with real liquidity
Any risk at all; a clean paper-trading result is a complete guarantee of live success
Data feed formatting issues
Infrastructure reliability issues
questions.explain: Because paper orders are simulated, they never actually move the market the way a real order of meaningful size would. This means market-impact risk (covered in Lesson 17) remains untested by paper trading, even when every other signal looks clean.
